title: Precedent and Persuasion
text:
Legal argumentation rests less on the mere invocation of statutes than on the careful reconciliation of competing precedents. Judges frequently confront a lacuna in the codified law, and they must then resort to analogical reasoning, extrapolating principles from earlier rulings to the novel facts before them. Such reasoning is seldom mechanical; it demands a nuanced appreciation of the ratio decidendi, the proposition that was genuinely necessary to the earlier outcome, as opposed to incidental remarks (obiter dicta) that carry merely persuasive weight.

Advocates, for their part, construct arguments that anticipate the opposing side's most formidable objection and neutralise it in advance. A well-crafted submission distinguishes adverse authority on its facts, or contends that the earlier decision was confined to a particular statutory context. Ultimately, the persuasiveness of a legal argument depends not only on its doctrinal soundness but also on its coherence with the broader principles that the court is evidently inclined to uphold.

questions.text: According to the passage, what must judges do when the codified law contains a lacuna?
options: They refuse to decide the case until the legislature acts.
They apply analogical reasoning, drawing principles from earlier rulings.
They rely solely on incidental remarks from past judgments.
They set aside precedent and decide by personal conviction.

questions.text: What does the passage say advocates do to counter the opposing side's strongest objection?
options: They ignore it, because it is rarely raised in court.
They concede the point entirely to save time.
They anticipate it and neutralise it in advance.
They ask the court to postpone the hearing.

questions.text: What can be inferred about obiter dicta from the passage?
options: They are binding on every later court in the same way as the ratio decidendi.
They are not essential to the earlier outcome, so they carry weaker authority.
They are the most important part of any judgment.
They can only be found in statutes.

questions.text: The passage implies that a court's acceptance of an argument depends most on which factor?
options: The number of statutes cited in the submission.
The length of the written submission.
The seniority of the advocate presenting it.
Its coherence with principles the court is inclined to uphold.

paragraph_translations: El razonamiento jurídico descansa menos en la mera invocación de los estatutos que en la conciliación cuidadosa de precedentes contrapuestos. Los jueces se enfrentan con frecuencia a una laguna en el derecho codificado y deben entonces recurrir al razonamiento analógico, extrapolando principios de resoluciones anteriores a los hechos inéditos que tienen ante sí. Tal razonamiento rara vez es mecánico; exige una apreciación matizada de la ratio decidendi, la proposición que era verdaderamente necesaria para el resultado anterior, a diferencia de las observaciones incidentales (obiter dicta) que tienen un peso meramente persuasivo.

Los abogados, por su parte, construyen argumentos que anticipan la objeción más formidable de la parte contraria y la neutralizan de antemano. Un escrito bien elaborado distingue la jurisprudencia adversa según sus hechos, o sostiene que la decisión anterior se circunscribía a un contexto legal particular. En última instancia, la persuasión de un argumento jurídico depende no solo de su solidez doctrinal, sino también de su coherencia con los principios más amplios que el tribunal se muestra evidentemente dispuesto a sostener.
